newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rwanda genocide anniversary as Hutus plan return.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide anniversary as Hutus plan return.

text.p: Therese Uwimana is just one of about 300,000 Hutu refugees still suffering in eastern Zaire three years after the start of the Rwandan genocide.
One of the century's greatest collective crimes caused her predicament as surely as it is transforming the lives of tens of millions of people in Central Africa's Great Lakes region.
The last three years of tumult and war have created winners, like Zaire's rebel leader Laurent Kabila, and losers like Uwimana, a 29-year-old Rwandan teacher.

The slaughter of about 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda began on April 6, 1994, and lasted nearly three months. For Uwimana the real anniversary will come in July, three years after she joined more than two million Hutus who fled into Zaire and Tanzania.
The genocide had failed because Ugandan-backed Tutsi rebels won the civil war, took power in Rwanda's capital Kigali and set to work to ensure their people would never be victims again.
"We were frightened and there was fighting so I took my children and my husband stayed behind in Cyangugu," Uwimana said at Kilometre 42, a refugee settlement south of Kisangani in rebel-held Zaire.
For two years and three months she taught in a refugee camp in Zaire but lived in relative comfort with missionaries in the attractive town of Bukavu, across the lake from her homeland.
"I was able to keep in touch with my husband from Bukavu and he said there were no problems for him in Cyangugu. But there was still too much insecurity for me to go back."

The bearable routine of life in the Hutu camps, controlled by armed ex-soldiers, militiamen and educated leaders who denied a genocide had ever happened, was funded by the international community at the rate of $1 million a day.
It ended last October when Kabila's rebels launched their revolt against Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Their first target was to clear the refugees away from the borders with Rwanda and Burundi, whose Tutsi-dominated armies supported the rebels and were repaid with the closure of hostile Hutu guerrilla bases in and around the camps.
Their second target was Mobutu, master of Central Africa until his rule started to wane in 1990 and who made the mistake of backing the Rwandan government that committed the genocide.
Kabila's men took more than a third of Zaire, Africa's third largest country and an Eldorado of minerals and diamonds.

"I left Bukavu on October 24, 1996, because of the fighting," Uwimana said. For more than five months she lived a nightmare with a group of at least 100,000 Hutus, walking as fast as possible to stay ahead of the advancing rebels.

Their plight led to calls for international intervention last November. The debate in world forums went on for weeks but the main advocate for the force, France, was mistrusted by the rebels and Rwanda because of its support for Mobutu.
The plan was blocked by other powers, including the United States, which denied the refugees were as numerous as the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR had calculated.
The wandering Hutus crossed rivers and pitiless expanses of volcanic rock before disappearing under a lightless canopy of tropical forest, surviving on plants, bark and insects.
Hundreds, perhaps thousands, died en route. An unknown number were killed by the rebels, some human rights groups say.
Aid workers think at least 300 died when they crossed the Lualaba River last month at Ubundu, 125 km (75 miles) south of Kisangani after trekking 600 km (375 miles) from Bukavu.

"We sold our shoes, even our last cooking pots to the boatmen to take us across in canoes. Those who had nothing tried to swim or made bamboo rafts but there was a sudden wind and many people drowned," said Uwimana.
After the crossing, most had had enough and decided to go to the rebels in Kisangani and seek repatriation, following the huge majority of the refugees who first fled Rwanda in 1994.
The UNHCR estimates there are still 300,000 Hutus stranded in Zaire with Uwimana's group the largest concentration.

The hardliners, including ex-soldiers and militiamen who face execution or prison if they go home, lost their hold. A few thousand set off deeper into the forest, hoping to reach government-held Opala.
"I think they want to become Zaireans but they don't want to fight anymore, they are too tired," said Uwimana.
For Rwanda's authorities, already detaining 100,000 Hutus as genocide suspects, the refugees like Uwimana's group who risked death to avoid repatriation must include the guiltiest.

Salvation of sorts came to Uwimana and the 100,000 refugees south of Kisangani, dying of hunger and malaria at the rate of at least 120 a day, when Kabila agreed on Saturday to allow relief agencies to mount a repatriation airlift.
The operation might take two months but the refugees all say they want to go home, whatever their fate.
"I'm not frightened to go back. I want to leave now, even tonight," said Uwimana.

Asked if he remembered it was the genocide anniversary, refugee Theobald Munyakayanza replied: "The life we're living here means we don't care anything about calendars. We still don't know what has happened to us and our country."
A teacher, he had five children with him after two died on the trek. On Sunday he adopted two more, orphans who were watching as their mother's body was prepared for burial.
"The problem is, everyone here has been accused of genocide and that is not fair. The guilty ones are in the bush and that is why they fled," he said.
